items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 15.6 A brass propeller. Brass is an alloy.

items.label: text
items.text: An alloy is a mixture of a metal with, usually, other metals or carbon. For example, brass is a mixture of copper and zinc, and steel is an alloy of iron with carbon.

items.label: text
items.text: Alloys are harder than the individual pure metals from which they are made. In an alloy, the different metals/elements have slightly differently sized atoms. This breaks up the regular lattice arrangement and makes it more difficult for the layers of ions to slide over each other.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 15.8 The layers cannot slide over each other as easily in an alloy as in a pure metal.

items.label: text
items.text: Remember, a metal consists of a regular lattice of metal ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons.

items.label: text
items.text: Other common alloys include bronze (a mixture of copper and tin), stainless steel (an alloy of iron with chromium and usually nickel), and the mixture of copper and nickel (cupronickel) which is usually used to make 'silver' coins.

items.label: section_header
items.text: PROPERTIES AND USES OF SOME METALS

items.label: text
items.text: Pure aluminium isn't very strong, so aluminium alloys are normally used instead. The aluminium can be strengthened by adding other elements, such as silicon, copper or magnesium.

items.label: caption
items.text: Figure 15.9 shows one of the uses of aluminium.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 15.9 Aluminium resists corrosion, it has a low density and is a good conductor of electricity. The aluminium in the cables in the photo is strengthened by a core of steel.

items.label: text
items.text: Other uses of aluminium include planes, electricity cables, and pots and pans. Its uses depend on its low density and strength (when alloyed), its ability to conduct electricity and heat, and its ability to resist corrosion.

items.label: text
items.text: Aluminium resists corrosion because it has a very thin, but very strong, layer of aluminium oxide on the surface. This prevents anything else reaching the surface and reacting with it.
